sections.name: General Knowledge
sections.note: Part 1 (VALR, DM, QADI) shares a combined 170-minute limit; GK is a separate 10-minute section with no negative marking.

items.passage: When a digital service is free, the user is often told that they are the customer. In practice they are frequently the product. The service is paid for by advertisers who want access to attention and data, and the design of the service follows the payer, not the user. Features that help advertisers target precisely are built first; features that help users leave, limit use, or understand what is collected are built late or not at all. This is not a conspiracy. It is the ordinary logic of who pays. A newspaper funded by readers serves readers; a newspaper funded by advertisers serves advertisers, and readers are the audience sold. The difference online is scale and precision: the audience can be sliced into thousands of segments and sold in real time. Some argue the bargain is fair, since users receive valuable services at no money cost. Others reply that the price is hidden, paid in privacy and in time spent on things the user never chose. The honest question is not whether free services are good or bad, but whether users understand the trade they are making and whether they have a real choice to make a different one.
items.question: The main argument of the passage is that
options: users never benefit from free services
advertisers should be banned from digital platforms
the design of a free service follows whoever pays for it
free digital services are a conspiracy against users
items.explanation: The passage states the design follows the payer, not the user, and explains this as ordinary logic of who pays. It explicitly denies a conspiracy, does not call for a ban, and acknowledges users receive valuable services.

items.question: The newspaper analogy is used to show that
options: readers have always been sold to advertisers
newspapers are more honest than websites
funding source shapes whom a service serves
items.explanation: The analogy contrasts a reader-funded newspaper serving readers with an advertiser-funded one serving advertisers, showing funding shapes service. It is not a claim about honesty, disappearance, or that readers were always sold.

items.question: According to the passage, what makes the online case different from the newspaper case?
options: The services are of lower quality
The audience can be segmented precisely and sold in real time
items.explanation: The passage says the difference online is scale and precision, with the audience sliced into thousands of segments and sold in real time. Quality, money cost and advertiser influence are not the stated difference.

items.question: The author would most likely support which of the following?
options: Removing all free services from the internet
Making all digital services paid by subscription
Clearer disclosure of the trade users make and genuine alternatives
items.explanation: The passage ends by asking whether users understand the trade and whether they have a real choice, implying support for transparency and alternatives. It does not advocate subscriptions for all, a ban, or removal of free services.

items.passage: A city is often described as a machine, with roads as pipes and buildings as parts. The metaphor misleads. Machines are designed once and then maintained; cities are redesigned daily by the people who use them. A shortcut worn through a park, a market that gathers at a bus stop, a lane that becomes a food street after dark: none of these was in the master plan, yet each reveals what residents actually need. Planners who ignore this informal redesign build places that look orderly on paper and feel dead on the ground. Planners who study it learn faster than any survey, because behaviour is honest in a way opinions are not. This does not mean planning is useless. Without sewers, grids and transport, the informal city cannot function at scale. The skill lies in building a strong skeleton and leaving room for the flesh to grow: wide pavements that can host stalls, squares that can be markets or playgrounds, rules that permit adaptation instead of freezing a single use. The best cities are not finished products. They are frameworks that invite their residents to keep finishing them.
items.question: Why does the author reject the machine metaphor for cities?
options: Buildings are not made of parts
Cities are redesigned daily by their users
Roads cannot be compared to pipes
Machines are too expensive to maintain
items.explanation: The passage says machines are designed once and maintained, while cities are redesigned daily by the people who use them. Cost, the pipe comparison and building parts are not the objection.

items.question: The worn shortcut through a park is cited as an example of
options: behaviour revealing what residents actually need
items.explanation: The passage lists the shortcut as informal redesign revealing what residents need, and says behaviour is honest. It is not framed as maintenance failure, lawbreaking or road failure.

items.question: The author's prescription for planners is to
options: freeze each area to a single use
build a strong skeleton and leave room for adaptation
items.explanation: The passage prescribes a strong skeleton with room for the flesh to grow and rules that permit adaptation. Abandoning plans, more surveys and freezing uses all contradict the argument.

items.question: Which statement would the author most likely agree with?
options: Orderly appearance on paper guarantees a lively city
Transport and sewers matter less than markets
Residents should never alter planned spaces
Informal uses of space are a reliable source of planning insight
items.explanation: The author says planners who study informal redesign learn faster than any survey. Orderly paper plans are said to feel dead, infrastructure is called essential, and alteration is welcomed, so the other options are opposite to the view.

items.question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
items.explanation: The correct spelling is occurrence, with double c and double r. The other forms drop a letter or add a wrong vowel.

items.question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
items.explanation: The correct spelling is accommodate, with double c and double m. The other options miss one of the doubled letters.

items.question: The sentences below form a paragraph when arranged correctly. Choose the correct order. (1) The idea spread quickly to other towns. (2) It began with a single library that lent tools instead of books. (3) Within a year, residents were borrowing drills, ladders and sewing machines. (4) Today, dozens of such libraries operate across the region.
items.explanation: The paragraph must start with the origin in sentence 2, then the early result in 3, then the spread in 1, then the present state in 4. Any order starting with 1 or 3 breaks the chronological flow from origin to expansion.

items.question: Arrange the sentences in logical order. (1) The river flooded the low fields every monsoon. (2) Farmers therefore built raised beds and small bunds. (3) Over time, yields became steadier despite heavy rain. (4) The bunds slowed the water and kept the soil in place.
items.explanation: The problem comes first in 1, the response in 2, the mechanism in 4, and the outcome in 3. Placing the response or mechanism before the problem breaks the cause and effect chain.

items.question: Arrange the sentences in logical order. (1) The committee published its findings on Friday. (2) It had interviewed more than two hundred residents. (3) The report recommended three concrete reforms. (4) The interviews began in January and lasted four months.
items.explanation: The logical flow is the interviews in 2, their timing in 4, publication in 1, then the recommendations in 3. Starting with publication or recommendations before the work is described breaks the sequence.

items.question: Which sentence best concludes this paragraph? 'Online reviews help buyers compare products, but a review is only as useful as it is honest. Fake reviews, paid praise and coordinated attacks distort the signal on which buyers rely.'
options: Online shopping should be banned to stop fake reviews.
Reviews are the only factor buyers should consider.
Buyers should therefore ignore all reviews completely.
Platforms and buyers must therefore protect the honesty of reviews for them to remain useful.
items.explanation: The paragraph argues reviews are useful only if honest and are distorted by fakes, so protecting honesty is the fitting conclusion. Ignoring all reviews, banning shopping and treating reviews as the only factor all go beyond or against the argument.

items.question: Statement: A city reduced bus fares by half and ridership rose by 40 percent in six months. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Bus fares are now too low to sustain the service
Every new rider previously travelled by car
Lower fares caused at least part of the rise in ridership
Ridership will keep rising by 40 percent every six months
items.explanation: A 40 percent rise following a fare cut supports lower fares contributing to the rise, though other factors cannot be ruled out. The data says nothing about previous car use, sustainability or future growth rates.

items.question: Argument: 'We should extend library hours because students asked for it in a survey.' What is the strongest objection?
options: Survey demand alone does not show the extension is affordable or the best use of funds
Students also asked for more computers
Some students do not use the library
items.explanation: The strongest objection challenges the inference from demand to action by raising cost and alternatives. Non-use by some students and the computer request do not undermine the case, and quietness is irrelevant.

items.question: If all managers are leaders, and some leaders are mentors, which follows with certainty?
options: No conclusion about managers and mentors follows with certainty
items.explanation: Some leaders are mentors does not guarantee the overlap falls among managers, who are only a subset of leaders. The premises do not fix where the mentor overlap lies, so no manager-mentor conclusion is certain.

items.question: If no honest person lies, and some politicians lie, what follows?
items.explanation: If some politicians lie and no honest person lies, those lying politicians cannot be honest. The premises do not show all politicians lie or that no politician is honest.

items.question: Choose the pair that best expresses a relationship similar to Author : Book.
options: All of these express a creator and creation
items.explanation: An author creates a book, a painter creates a painting on canvas, a singer performs a song, and a chef creates a dish from a recipe, but the cleanest shared relation is creator to creation. Among single pairs the creator-creation link holds, and the inclusive option captures that all three share it.

items.question: Book is to Reading as Fork is to
items.explanation: A book is the instrument of reading, and a fork is the instrument of eating. Drawing uses a pencil, stirring uses a spoon, and cooking is a broader activity rather than the fork's direct use.

items.question: Find the odd one out.
items.explanation: Novel, poem and essay are all forms of writing, while a library is a place where writings are kept. The first three share the category of literary form, and library belongs to a different category.

items.question: Find the odd one out.
items.explanation: Copper, iron and aluminium are pure metals, while steel is an alloy made mainly from iron and carbon. The distinction is elemental metal versus alloy, so steel is the odd one out.

items.question: Which word can fill both blanks? 'The lawyer presented a ______ argument. The evidence was ______ and hard to dispute.'
items.explanation: Compelling fits both a strong argument and evidence that is hard to dispute. Weak and confusing contradict the second sentence, and lengthy describes size rather than force.

items.question: Which word can fill both blanks? 'The new policy was ______ in its first month. Officials called the early results ______.'
items.explanation: Promising fits both early success and officials describing early results positively. Disappointing and unclear contradict positive early results, and controversial is not supported by the context.

items.question: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to cut corners'.
options: To do something cheaply by skipping steps
To take the shortest physical route
items.explanation: To cut corners means to do something in the easiest or cheapest way by omitting steps, often at the cost of quality. It is not about physical routes, equal division or blunt speech.

items.question: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to hit the nail on the head'.
items.explanation: The idiom means to say exactly the right thing or identify the precise issue. It does not refer to injury, starting a task or arguing loudly.

items.passage: A pharmaceutical firm sells a life-saving drug at a high price in a wealthy market, which funds research. A low-income country asks for the same drug at a much lower price, arguing that patients will die without it. Offering the low price risks parallel imports back into the wealthy market and anger from shareholders who see revenue fall.
items.question: Which approach best balances access and sustainability?
options: Offer a tiered price with safeguards against diversion, such as distinct packaging and controlled distribution
Refuse any price cut to protect research funding
Give the drug free to everyone immediately
Raise the wealthy-market price to cover the discount
items.explanation: Tiered pricing with anti-diversion safeguards expands access while protecting the revenue that funds research. Refusal leaves patients without treatment, free supply for all is unsustainable, and raising the wealthy price does not address diversion.

items.question: The risk of parallel imports is best managed by
options: Distinct packaging, batch tracking, and agreements with distributors
Charging the same high price everywhere
Refusing to sell in the low-income country
Ignoring it and hoping it does not happen
items.explanation: Distinct packaging, batch tracking and distributor agreements directly reduce diversion while preserving access. Ignoring the risk, refusing to sell, and uniform high pricing all avoid the problem rather than managing it.

items.question: Shareholder concern about falling revenue should be addressed by
options: Promising the discount is temporary without a plan
Explaining the volume, reputation and long-term market benefits of tiered access
items.explanation: Explaining volume, reputation and long-term market benefits gives shareholders a reasoned basis to support access. Hiding, empty promises and cancelling research all damage trust or the firm's future.

items.passage: A bank's loan-approval algorithm rejects applicants from certain neighbourhoods at a much higher rate. The data team says the model only uses income, repayment history and loan size, and the pattern reflects historical data. The compliance head warns the pattern may amount to indirect discrimination and reputational harm.
items.question: What should the bank do first?
options: Keep using the model, since it does not use neighbourhood directly
Pause and audit the model for proxy variables and disparate impact before further use
Lower the approval threshold for everyone
items.explanation: Pausing to audit for proxy variables and disparate impact tests whether neutral inputs reproduce a discriminatory pattern. Continuing, deleting data and blanket threshold cuts all avoid the diagnosis the bank needs.

items.question: The data team's defence is weak because
options: neutral inputs can act as proxies for protected characteristics through correlated patterns
items.explanation: Income, history and loan size can correlate with neighbourhood and other protected characteristics, so a model can discriminate indirectly without using the protected label. Historical data is not always wrong, algorithms are useful, and income is relevant.

items.question: A responsible long-term fix would include
options: Hiding the approval criteria from applicants
Removing all data and deciding by intuition
Regular fairness audits, explainable criteria, and a human review route for rejected applicants
items.explanation: Regular fairness audits, explainable criteria and human review make the system checkable and correctable. Intuition, blanket approval and hidden criteria all remove accountability rather than adding it.

items.passage: A consumer goods firm plans to label a product as environmentally friendly because one ingredient is sustainably sourced, although the product's overall footprint is high and its packaging is not recyclable. Marketing expects a sales lift; the sustainability officer warns the claim could be seen as misleading.
items.question: What should the firm do about the label?
options: Drop all sustainability work to avoid scrutiny
Label every product as friendly to stay competitive
Use a precise claim about the one ingredient only, with the full footprint disclosed
Use the label as planned, since one ingredient is sustainable
items.explanation: A precise claim about the one ingredient plus full footprint disclosure is truthful and lets buyers judge. The broad friendly label overstates the case, dropping the work avoids progress, and labelling everything compounds the deception.

items.question: The marketing expectation of a sales lift is not a good reason to use the broad label because
options: a short-term lift can become a lasting trust loss if buyers feel misled
items.explanation: A lift built on a misleading claim risks lasting trust loss and regulatory action when buyers learn the full picture. Marketing can promote truthfully, sustainable ingredients can sell, and regulators do check claims.

items.question: Which evidence would best support a genuine environmental claim?
options: A competitor using the same label
A full lifecycle assessment with independent verification
An internal memo praising the product
items.explanation: A full lifecycle assessment with independent verification tests the whole footprint rather than one ingredient. Competitor practice, one review and an internal memo are not evidence of overall impact.

items.passage: A pharmaceutical company funds a free health clinic in a small town, covering staff salaries and equipment. Its representatives visit often and suggest the company's own branded medicines. The clinic director notices prescriptions of the sponsor's drug rising sharply, even when cheaper generics are equally effective. A local doctor asks the director to act. The sponsor hints that funding will be reviewed if its products are not given a fair chance.
items.question: What should the director do first?
options: Ask the sponsor to increase funding in exchange for more prescriptions
Tell doctors to prescribe generics without any explanation
Ban the sponsor's drug outright from the clinic
Separate prescribing decisions from funding by setting an independent formulary committee
items.explanation: The first step is to separate clinical judgement from funding by creating an independent formulary committee that decides on medical merit. Taking more funding for prescriptions would trade patient welfare for money, an outright ban overreacts without evidence, and unexplained orders to doctors solve nothing.

items.question: The sponsor's argument that its funding entitles it to influence prescriptions is weak because
options: The clinic is located in a small town
Funding a clinic does not buy clinical judgement, which must serve patients, not donors
Generics are always cheaper than branded drugs
items.explanation: A donation funds a service; it does not purchase the right to steer treatment. Clinical judgement must serve patients, and letting a funder direct prescriptions would breach that duty. The town's size, the price of generics and doctors' paperwork preferences are irrelevant to the argument.

items.question: Which safeguard best protects patients in the long term?
options: Publish the clinic's prescribing policy and audit prescriptions against it
Keep the sponsor's visits secret from patients
Ask the sponsor to fund a new building instead
Let each doctor decide privately with no oversight
items.explanation: A published prescribing policy plus regular audits makes decisions transparent and checkable, which is the durable protection. Secrecy and purely private decisions hide the problem, and a new building does nothing about prescribing.

items.passage: A consulting team realises a client report will be late because a key data source was delayed. The client has a board meeting the next day and is counting on the report. The team can deliver an incomplete draft on time, deliver a complete report a day late, or present the draft as complete and fix errors later.
items.question: What should the team do?
options: Tell the client now, deliver the best accurate draft on time labelled as draft, with the complete report to follow
Blame the data provider and refuse to deliver anything
Present the draft as complete and fix errors later
Say nothing and deliver late without warning
items.explanation: Early honesty plus an accurately labelled draft gives the client something usable for the board meeting without misleading them. Presenting a draft as complete is deception, silence leaves the client unprepared, and blaming without delivery abandons the client.

items.question: Presenting the draft as complete is wrong primarily because it
options: deprives the client of the chance to plan around the gaps
items.explanation: The core harm is that the client cannot plan around gaps they do not know exist, so board decisions may rest on incomplete work. Effort, speed and provider feelings are secondary to the client's ability to decide knowingly.

items.question: What should the team change for the next engagement?
options: Promise earlier deadlines to impress clients
Build buffer time for data delays and agree escalation triggers with the client in advance
items.explanation: Buffer time and agreed escalation triggers address the root cause, which was a single-point delay with no plan. Earlier promises, avoiding external data and hiding delays all repeat or worsen the failure.

items.passage: An employee finds evidence that a factory is discharging waste above permitted limits at night. The plant manager is a respected figure who has won awards for safety. The employee fears retaliation and job loss, but the discharge harms a nearby river used by villagers.
items.question: What should the employee do?
options: Do nothing to protect their job
Use the firm's confidential reporting channel, and if that fails, approach the regulator with evidence
Confront the plant manager alone at night
Leak the evidence to the press first without any internal step
items.explanation: A confidential internal channel first, then the regulator if that fails, gives the firm a chance to act while protecting the employee and creating a record. Doing nothing leaves the harm in place, a lone night confrontation is unsafe, and going straight to the press skips a safer remedy.

items.question: The plant manager's awards are irrelevant to the decision because
options: villagers do not care about awards
past good performance does not excuse current harm to the river
items.explanation: Awards reflect past performance and do not make current unlawful discharge acceptable or harmless. The point is not that awards are undeserved or ignored, but that they cannot offset present harm.

items.question: What should the firm do once the report is received?
options: Punish the reporting employee for disloyalty
Investigate independently, stop the discharge, and protect the reporter from retaliation
Transfer the reporter to another site quietly
items.explanation: Independent investigation, stopping the discharge and protecting the reporter address the harm and the fear that suppresses reporting. Punishing, quietly transferring or waiting all preserve the harm and deter future reports.

items.passage: A subscription app offers a free trial that converts to a paid plan unless the user cancels. Many users forget to cancel and are charged. The growth team wants to keep the design because it converts well; the product head worries it exploits forgetfulness and will damage trust when users notice the charge.
items.question: What design best balances growth and trust?
options: Send clear reminders before conversion, make cancellation easy, and require explicit confirmation to continue
Charge users before the trial starts
items.explanation: Reminders, easy cancellation and explicit confirmation let users choose knowingly while still converting those who value the service. Keeping the trap, hiding cancellation and charging early all exploit inattention rather than earning renewal.

items.question: The growth team's conversion argument is incomplete because it
options: ignores the cost of refunds and churn when users feel tricked
items.explanation: High conversion from forgetfulness brings refunds, complaints and churn when users feel tricked, which the raw conversion rate hides. Product quality and features are not what the argument omits.

items.question: Which metric should the firm watch alongside conversion?
options: Voluntary renewal after the first paid month and complaint rates
items.explanation: Voluntary renewal and complaint rates reveal whether conversions reflect genuine value or trickery. Downloads, rent and feature counts do not distinguish willing subscribers from trapped ones.

items.question: A price is increased by 25% and then decreased by 20%. What is the net percentage change in the price?
items.explanation: Take the price as 100. After a 25% increase it is 125, and a 20% decrease on 125 gives 125 x 0.80 = 100, so there is no net change. Adding 25% and subtracting 20% to get 5% is wrong because the decrease applies to the higher price.

items.question: What is the highest common factor of 24 and 36?
items.explanation: The factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24 and of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. The largest common factor is 12.

items.question: What is the simple interest on Rs 5000 for 3 years at 8% per annum?
items.explanation: Simple interest is P x R x T / 100 = 5000 x 8 x 3 / 100 = Rs 1200. The interest grows linearly with time, so three years at 8 percent gives 24 percent of the principal, which is Rs 1200.

items.question: What is the average of the first 10 natural numbers?
items.explanation: The sum of the first 10 natural numbers is 10 x 11 / 2 = 55, and the average is 55/10 = 5.5.

items.question: The ratio of A to B is 3:5 and their sum is 64. What is the value of A?
items.explanation: The ratio parts total 3 + 5 = 8, so one part is 64/8 = 8, and A is 3 x 8 = 24. B would be 5 x 8 = 40, and 24 + 40 = 64, which checks the answer.

items.question: A can do a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. Working together, how many days will they take?
items.explanation: A does 1/10 and B does 1/15 per day, so together they do 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 per day, giving 6 days.

items.question: A train 180 metres long running at 54 km/h crosses a pole. How long does it take?
items.explanation: 54 km/h is 15 m/s, so the time is 180/15 = 12 seconds. Converting km/h to m/s means multiplying by 5/18, and forgetting the conversion is the usual error here.

items.question: What is the compound interest on Rs 8000 for 2 years at 10% per annum?
items.explanation: The amount is 8000 x 1.1 x 1.1 = Rs 9680, so the interest is 9680 - 8000 = Rs 1680.

items.question: A shopkeeper buys an article for Rs 250 and sells it for Rs 300. What is his profit percentage?
items.explanation: Profit is 300 - 250 = Rs 50 on a cost of Rs 250, so 50/250 x 100 = 20%. The profit percentage is always calculated on the cost price, not on the selling price.

items.question: A boat goes downstream at 12 km/h and upstream at 8 km/h. What is the speed of the boat in still water?
items.explanation: Still water speed is the average of downstream and upstream speeds, (12 + 8)/2 = 10 km/h.

items.question: If x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0, what is the sum of the roots?
items.explanation: The equation factors as (x - 2)(x - 3) = 0, so the roots are 2 and 3, and their sum is 5. By the formula, the sum is -b/a = 5.

items.question: In an arithmetic progression the first term is 5 and the common difference is 3. What is the 10th term?
items.explanation: The nth term is a + (n - 1)d = 5 + 9 x 3 = 32. The 10th term adds nine common differences to the first term, not ten, which is the common slip.

items.question: A coin is tossed 3 times. What is the probability of getting exactly 2 heads?
items.explanation: There are 8 equally likely outcomes. The outcomes with exactly two heads are HHT, HTH and THH, which is 3 outcomes, so the probability is 3/8.

items.question: A rectangle has length 12 cm and breadth 9 cm. What is the length of its diagonal?
items.explanation: By Pythagoras, the diagonal is sqrt(12^2 + 9^2) = sqrt(144 + 81) = sqrt(225) = 15 cm.

items.question: What is the remainder when 3^100 is divided by 7?
items.explanation: Modulo 7, powers of 3 cycle 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1 with period 6. Since 100 leaves remainder 4 on division by 6, 3^100 is congruent to the 4th value in the cycle, 4.

items.question: In how many ways can 6 books be arranged on a shelf if 2 particular books must always be together?
items.explanation: Treat the two books as one block, which can be arranged with the other four in 5! = 120 ways, and the two books inside the block can swap in 2 ways. Total is 120 x 2 = 240.

items.question: What is the area of a circle of radius 14 cm? (Use pi = 22/7)
items.explanation: Area is pi x r^2 = (22/7) x 14 x 14 = 22 x 28 = 616 sq cm. Because the radius 14 cancels the 7 in the denominator, the arithmetic stays clean with pi = 22/7.

items.question: If x + 1/x = 6, what is the value of x^2 + 1/x^2?
items.explanation: Squaring gives x^2 + 2 + 1/x^2 = 36, so x^2 + 1/x^2 = 34. The cross term 2 must be subtracted; forgetting it would wrongly give 36.

items.question: Two trains 150 m and 100 m long run towards each other at 60 km/h and 40 km/h. How long do they take to cross each other completely?
items.explanation: Relative speed is 60 + 40 = 100 km/h, which is 250/9 m/s. Total distance is 250 m, so time is 250 / (250/9) = 9 seconds.

items.question: A mixture has milk and water in the ratio 7:3. In 20 litres of the mixture, how much water must be added to make the ratio 7:5?
items.explanation: The mixture has 14 litres of milk and 6 litres of water. Let x litres of water be added: 14/(6 + x) = 7/5, so 70 = 42 + 7x, giving x = 4 litres.

items.question: What is the value of log3(81)?
items.explanation: 3^4 = 81, so log base 3 of 81 is 4. A logarithm asks for the exponent, and 3 raised to 4 is 81, while 3 raised to 3 is only 27.

items.question: What is the total surface area of a cube of side 6 cm?
items.explanation: A cube has 6 faces, each 6 x 6 = 36 sq cm, so the total surface area is 6 x 36 = 216 sq cm.

items.question: Which product had the highest total sales over the four months?

diagram.caption: Monthly sales (Rs lakh) of three products, Jan to Apr

items.explanation: Adding the four months: P = 40 + 50 + 60 + 70 = 220, Q = 30 + 45 + 55 + 70 = 200, R = 50 + 40 + 60 + 50 = 200. Product P has the highest total at Rs 220 lakh.

items.question: What is the percentage growth in Product P's sales from January to April?
items.explanation: Product P's sales rose from Rs 40 lakh in January to Rs 70 lakh in April, an increase of 30 lakh. The percentage growth is 30/40 x 100 = 75%.

items.question: In which month was the combined sales of all three products the highest, and by how much did it exceed the lowest month?
items.explanation: The combined totals are Jan = 120, Feb = 135, Mar = 175 and Apr = 190 lakh. The highest is Apr at 190 and the lowest is Jan at 120, so Apr exceeds Jan by 70 lakh.

items.question: What is the overall percentage increase in total enrolment from 2023 to 2024?

diagram.caption: Students enrolled in four courses, 2023 and 2024

items.explanation: Total enrolment in 2023 was 550 and in 2024 it was 610. The increase is 60 on a base of 550, which is 10.9%.

items.question: Which course recorded the highest percentage growth in enrolment?
items.explanation: Growth rates are: A 25.0%, B 37.5%, C 5.0%, D -6.7%. Course B has the highest percentage growth at 37.5%, even though other courses added similar absolute numbers on larger bases.

items.question: What is the ratio of Course C students to Course A students in 2024?
items.explanation: In 2024 Course C had 210 students and Course A had 150, so the ratio is 210:150. Dividing both sides by 30 gives 7:5.

items.question: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
items.explanation: Mars appears red because of iron oxide, or rust, on its surface. Venus is the hottest planet, Jupiter is the largest, and Mercury is the closest to the Sun.

items.question: Which is the smallest continent in the world?
items.explanation: Australia is the smallest continent by land area. Europe is the second smallest, Africa is the second largest, and Antarctica is larger than both Australia and Europe.

items.question: What is the capital of Australia?
items.explanation: Canberra is the capital of Australia. Sydney is the largest city, Melbourne is the second largest, and Perth is the capital of Western Australia.

items.question: What is the currency of Japan?
items.explanation: The yen is the currency of Japan. The won is used in Korea, the yuan in China, and the ringgit in Malaysia.

items.question: How many players are there in a cricket team on the field?
items.explanation: A cricket team fields 11 players. A football team also has 11 players, while a hockey team has 11 as well; 9 is the size of a baseball team.

items.question: Which instrument is used to measure temperature?
items.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature. A barometer measures atmospheric pressure, an altimeter measures altitude, and a speedometer measures speed.

items.question: The headquarters of the International Monetary Fund is located in which city?
items.explanation: The IMF is headquartered in Washington DC, United States, as is the World Bank. New York hosts the UN headquarters, Geneva hosts the WHO, and Paris hosts UNESCO.

items.question: Who wrote 'A Brief History of Time'?
items.explanation: Stephen Hawking wrote 'A Brief History of Time' in 1988. Carl Sagan wrote 'Cosmos', Einstein wrote on relativity, and Feynman wrote the famous Lectures on Physics.

items.question: Which is the longest river in India?
items.explanation: The Ganga is the longest river in India at about 2,525 km. The Godavari is the longest peninsular river, the Brahmaputra is longer overall but most of its course lies outside India, and the Yamuna is a tributary of the Ganga.

items.question: Which Indian state is the largest by area?
items.explanation: Rajasthan is the largest Indian state by area, about 3.42 lakh sq km. Madhya Pradesh is second, Maharashtra third, and Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state.

items.question: Who was the first President of India?
options: Dr A P J Abdul Kalam
items.explanation: Dr Rajendra Prasad was the first President of India, serving from 1950 to 1962. Radhakrishnan was the second President, Kalam the eleventh, and Zail Singh the seventh.

items.question: Which article of the Indian Constitution deals with the abolition of untouchability?
items.explanation: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. Article 14 is equality before law, Article 19 lists freedoms, and Article 21 protects life and personal liberty.

items.question: The Battle of Plassey was fought in which year?
items.explanation: The Battle of Plassey was fought in 1757 between the British East India Company and the Nawab of Bengal, marking the start of British political control in India. Buxar was fought in 1764 and the revolt of 1857 came a century later.

items.question: Who discovered penicillin?
items.explanation: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928. Pasteur developed germ theory and vaccines, Lister pioneered antiseptic surgery, and Koch identified the bacteria causing tuberculosis and cholera.

items.question: Which is the largest lake in India?
items.explanation: Wular Lake in Jammu and Kashmir is the largest freshwater lake in India. Chilika in Odisha is the largest brackish water lagoon, Sambhar in Rajasthan is a salt lake, and Dal Lake is also in Kashmir but smaller.

items.question: The headquarters of the World Health Organization is located in which city?
items.explanation: The WHO is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. New York hosts the UN headquarters, Paris hosts UNESCO, and Vienna hosts the IAEA and OPEC.

items.question: Who is known as the Iron Man of India?
items.explanation: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel is called the Iron Man of India for integrating the princely states into the Union. Bose led the INA, Bhagat Singh was a revolutionary, and Lala Lajpat Rai was the Lion of Punjab.

items.question: Which state is the largest producer of rice in India?
items.explanation: West Bengal is the largest producer of rice in India. Punjab is a major rice producer too but ranks below West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh is second in some years, and Tamil Nadu is a smaller producer.

items.question: The 'Quit India Movement' was launched in which year?
items.explanation: The Quit India Movement was launched by Mahatma Gandhi in August 1942. The Non-Cooperation Movement began in 1920, the Salt March in 1930, and independence came in 1947.

items.question: Which gas do plants absorb from the atmosphere during photosynthesis?
items.explanation: Plants absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen during photosynthesis. Oxygen is released, not absorbed; nitrogen is fixed from soil by bacteria, and hydrogen is not absorbed as a gas.

items.question: Who wrote 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money'?
items.explanation: John Maynard Keynes published 'The General Theory' in 1936, founding macroeconomics. Adam Smith wrote 'The Wealth of Nations', Ricardo wrote on comparative advantage, and Friedman led the monetarist school.

items.question: Which schedule of the Indian Constitution contains the list of official languages?
items.explanation: The Eighth Schedule lists the 22 scheduled languages of India. The Seventh Schedule divides powers between Union and states, the Ninth Schedule protects certain laws from judicial review, and the Tenth Schedule deals with defection.

items.question: The term 'Hindu rate of growth' was coined by which economist?
items.explanation: Raj Krishna coined the term 'Hindu rate of growth' for India's slow growth of about 3.5 percent a year before the 1980s. Amartya Sen worked on welfare economics, Bhagwati on trade, and K N Raj on planning.

items.question: Who was the first Indian woman to become President of the United Nations General Assembly?
items.explanation: Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit became President of the UN General Assembly in 1953, the first woman to hold the post. Sarojini Naidu was the first Indian woman governor, Indira Gandhi was Prime Minister, and Lakshmi Sahgal was an INA officer.

items.question: Which country is the largest producer of lithium in the world?
items.explanation: Australia is the world's largest producer of lithium, mined from hard rock, ahead of Chile, which has the largest reserves in salt flats. China processes much of the world's lithium but produces less from mines.
